At 3:17 every morning, the lighthouse went dark.

No one in the village noticed at first. Why would they? The lighthouse stood on an island two miles from shore, where the sea gnawed black rocks into blacker sand. Its beam turned faithfully across bedroom windows and empty streets, sweeping over the harbor, the cliffs, and the old churchyard.

But for eleven seconds each night, it vanished.

Mara noticed because she had stopped sleeping.

She was seventeen, furious at the world, and tired in a way that felt older than tiredness. Her brother had gone to sea six months earlier and had not returned. The villagers called it an accident, then a tragedy, then—when grief became inconvenient—“what happened.”

Mara called it impossible.

Elias knew the currents. He knew the reefs. He knew every mood of the northern wind. He had once steered home through fog so thick that the bow of his boat seemed to have been cut from the rest of the world.

He would not simply disappear.

So Mara stayed awake. She sat beside her window with a blanket around her shoulders and watched the lighthouse beam comb the darkness.

At 3:17, it failed.

One.

Two.

Three.

She counted to eleven.

Then the light returned.

The next night, the same.

On the seventh night, Mara stole a rowboat.

The sea was calm but not kind. It nudged her off course, tested her hands, slipped cold fingers over the gunwales. By the time she reached the island, her palms were bleeding.

The lighthouse door was unlocked.

Inside, a spiral staircase rose through darkness. Mara climbed past rusted pipes and portraits of former keepers. All of them looked stern except one: a young woman with wild hair and a smile that suggested she knew a secret.

At the top, Mara found the keeper asleep in a chair.

He was ancient, even by village standards, with a white beard spread over his chest. Beside him, enormous brass gears turned the lamp. Each tooth caught the next with soft, oily precision.

Mara watched the clock.

3:16.

“Wake up,” she said.

The keeper snored.

She shook him.

His eyes opened instantly.

“You shouldn’t be here,” he said.

3:17.

The lamp went dark.

Beyond the glass, the night changed.

Where the sea had been empty, lights now floated beneath the water—hundreds of them, green and gold, moving like lanterns carried along a submerged road.

Among them sailed ships.

Some were broken. Some were ancient, with sails swollen by winds that did not touch the surface. Some were little more than shadows. They passed silently below, traveling toward a pale opening in the depths.

And there, standing in the bow of a blue fishing boat, was Elias.

Mara struck the glass with both hands.

“Elias!”

His head turned.

For one second, he saw her.

He smiled—not like a ghost, not like a memory, but like her brother. Then he pointed toward the lamp.

The light returned.

The underwater road disappeared.

Mara spun toward the keeper. “Bring it back.”

“I can’t.”

“You turned it off.”

“No. It turns itself off.”

“Then break it.”

“You don’t understand.”

She seized a metal stool and raised it over the gears.

The keeper caught her wrist with surprising strength.

“The light keeps the dead from seeing the shore,” he said.

Mara froze.

“They travel on,” he continued, “because they cannot see what they’ve left behind. For eleven seconds, the machinery falters. Sometimes they look up. Sometimes the living look down. That is permitted.”

“By whom?”

The keeper glanced at the vast darkness outside.

“Not everything needs a name.”

Mara lowered the stool.

Below them, waves pressed against the island. The lamp continued its turning, steady and bright.

“Is he dead?” she asked.

The keeper’s face softened. “He is gone.”

“That isn’t the same answer.”

“No.”

“Where are they going?”

“Somewhere we cannot follow by boat.”

Mara hated him then. She hated his riddles, his resignation, the tenderness in his voice. Most of all she hated that Elias had smiled. She had spent six months imagining him afraid, injured, calling for help. She had carried his terror because she believed no one else would.

But he had not looked afraid.

“Can I see him again?”

“Tomorrow,” said the keeper. “For eleven seconds.”

So Mara returned the next night.

And the next.

Sometimes Elias’s boat passed near the island. Sometimes it was far below, no larger than a blue coin. Each night he waved. Each night Mara tried to memorize him: the slope of his shoulders, the curl of his hair, the patched sleeve of his coat.

Then, one night, his boat approached the pale opening.

Mara knew he would not return.

At 3:16, she placed her hand against the glass.

The lamp went dark.

The drowned road appeared, brighter than ever. Elias stood at the bow. He did not wave this time. He only looked at her.

Mara had prepared a hundred things to say. That she missed him. That their mother still set three plates at supper. That his dog slept outside his room. That she was angry. That she was sorry. That she had not known how large the world was until he left it.

Eleven seconds was not enough.

So she said only, “Go.”

Elias nodded.

His boat entered the light.

The lamp returned, and the sea was only sea.

Years later, villagers would speak of Mara as the finest lighthouse keeper the coast had ever known. She polished the lens until it shone like ice. She kept the gears oiled, the windows clear, and the great beam turning through storm and fog.

Sailors trusted her light.

But at 3:17 every morning, she stood beside the glass as darkness gathered for eleven impossible seconds.

She never saw Elias again.

She saw others.

And whenever they looked up, frightened by the road ahead, Mara raised one hand from the shore they had lost.

Then she smiled.
